findings.why: 'Acne relief' is treatment language: it presents the products as treating a condition. 'Rapid' adds an unsubstantiated time-bound promise (CLM-07).
This claims a cosmetic reduces scarring, which overstates what it can do and edges toward a treatment claim. Scope it to appearance.
findings.fix: Helps reduce the look of acne marks

findings.why: The ad is labelled brand-authored for Minimalist but promotes Dot & Key. Running it would misattribute the products, so confirm the advertiser before review.
findings.fix: Route this ad out of the Minimalist review, or replace the brand and product references with the correct Minimalist ones.

rule_hit_review.why: 'Treats Acne' is an explicit drug claim on a cosmetic. 'Super-Effectively' adds an unsubstantiated superlative.
'Get acne-free skin' promises an end to acne, an elimination claim on the cosmetic/drug line. It's also an absolute result (CLM-03).
'No Nasties' is clean-is-safe framing that implies other ingredients are harmful. It's a safety absolute the brand's philosophy rejects.
'Clinically Proven Results' needs a specific product study on file, with what was measured stated on the creative.
'Dermatologically Tested' is an endorsement-style claim that needs the test on file. Use the narrower 'patch tested under dermatological supervision' if that's what was done.
Checkmark emoji bullets (✅, ✔️) throughout are a competitor-category signature.

tone_read: This is a category-style ad: checkmark-emoji bullets, a 'Treats Acne Super-Effectively' headline and claims stacked without explanation. It's the opposite of Minimalist's calm, educational voice.
language_read: CICA is named without any concentration, efficacy is unhedged throughout ('Minimizes', 'Rapid acne relief', 'Uncompromised Efficacy'), and 'real CICA leaves' plus 'No Nasties' lean on natural/clean framing the brand avoids.
